name: Preposition Phrase
pattern: Head:P (+ Obj:NP / PredComp:NP/AdjP / Comp:PP/AdvP/clause; or no complement)

entry.name: Preposition Phrase
entry.pattern: Head:P (+ Obj:NP / PredComp:NP/AdjP / Comp:PP/AdvP/clause; or no complement)

dimensions.form: Phrase headed by a preposition; NP complements may be objects or predicatives, and PP, AdvP, or clause complements are also licensed
dimensions.meaning: Relates an entity or situation to another in space, time, comparison, reason, or abstract structure
dimensions.function: Complement, modifier, adjunct, or predicative complement in a containing construction
dimensions.distribution: Complement of verbs and nouns, modifier in NPs and clauses, and complement of prepositions

1.definition: Phrase headed by a preposition, with or without a complement
1.details: The head may take an NP object (in the garden), a predicative NP or AdjP (as a liability, as reasonable), an AdvP (until recently), a clause (because it rained), a PP (from under the bed), or no complement (outside). A single complementless preposition constitutes a complete PP (CGEL Ch. 2 §7, p. 58).

examples.note: P with PP complement; under the bed expresses the source location
Complete PP consisting of one complementless preposition

constraints.description: The phrase is headed by a preposition; locative members accept such modifiers as right and straight.

projection.target: A preposition can head a phrase even without an NP after it, as in We waited outside. Some heads take a different category, as with because it rained, and a PP can itself be selected, as with from under the stairs.
projection.evidence: CGEL classifies PPs by their heads and documents complement types and functions rather than identifying them through the presence of an NP alone.

curious.title: Phrases built around words like in and until
curious.summary: A preposition phrase is a group of words whose main word is a preposition, such as in, as, until or because.
curious.body:
In in the garden, the preposition in is the main word, and the garden follows it. The same kind of phrase can be built with other kinds of follower: as a liability, until recently, because it rained, and from under the bed.

A preposition can also stand alone as a complete phrase. Outside is a whole phrase on its own, as in We waited outside. What makes each of these a preposition phrase is its main word, not the kind of word that comes after it.
curious.try: Pick a short preposition like in, until or because. What can you put after it to make a phrase?

teacher.summary: Defines the PP and the range of complements a preposition can take, including none.
teacher.explain: A PP is a phrase headed by a preposition, with or without a complement. The head may take an NP object (in the garden), a predicative NP or AdjP (as a liability, as reasonable), an AdvP (until recently), a clause (because it rained), a PP (from under the bed), or no complement (outside). A single complementless preposition constitutes a complete PP. PPs are classified by their heads, not by an NP being present. Locative members accept modifiers such as right and straight. A PP can function as a complement, modifier, adjunct or predicative complement in a larger construction.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars sometimes treat words like outside, until and because as adverbs or conjunctions when no NP follows. Here each is a preposition heading a PP.

contrasts.note: A complete PP with no complement.

watch_for: A learner might think a preposition needs an NP after it, when outside can be a complete phrase.
A learner might analyze because it rained as a clause only, when this dictionary takes because as the head of a PP with a clause complement.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of PPs (in the garden, until recently, outside). They underline the preposition, then say what, if anything, follows it.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Preposition Phrase." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/pp-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, fa37529).
